name: Omar Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal shift look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 27, and I lead the afternoon call and chat shift at a contact centre. I have a two-year college diploma, and I handle the disputed bills junior agents cannot settle. I use an AI draft tool now and then, after someone else has shown me where it works. The best part is hearing a caller understand the fix before hanging up.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does work feel like when you get home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Usually steady. My pay is typical for this job, and my partner's bakery wage helps us keep about three months of expenses saved. I still notice when overtime disappears, because that is the part we use to build the reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the afternoon crew the shortcut tool is useful for simple address changes, nothing more. A caller with three wrong bills still needs somebody to stay on the line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my lead post is sound in this picture. My partner and I have about three months of expenses saved, though a quiet month of overtime would still pinch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep my regular shift and check the draft replies before they leave the centre. During the first year I'll put half of any overtime pay into our savings account, if overtime actually comes in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm calm about the work, mostly. I still watch our spending, but I don't see a reason to jump jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you and your partner use the savings account?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner works at a small bakery, so our wages don't rise and fall together. We agreed the savings account is for a real gap, not a holiday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where does the shortcut tool go wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I catch the tool mixing up account dates now and then. I'll use it for a draft, then read the record myself before promising a refund.

say: I'd say **simple address changes** can be drafted faster, but each draft still needs checking against the account.
I'd keep a **human agent** on tangled billing calls.
think: I expect my **lead post** to stay secure in this picture.
Our **three-month cushion** covers a short gap, though lost overtime would pinch.
do: Keep my **regular shift** and check drafted replies.
Save **half of overtime pay** if extra hours come in.
feel: **Calm** about work, with ordinary attention to spending.
S0.quote: A caller with three wrong bills still needs somebody to stay on the line.
fieldNote: His **three-month cushion** gives him room to keep his routine.
He treats **AI drafts** as useful only after checking account records.
His partner's **bakery wage** adds a separate source of household income.

steps.text: Keep leading the contact-centre shift and check AI drafts against account records
Save half of overtime pay if extra hours arise

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should measure what happens to the difficult calls before cutting seats. If easy chats vanish, the old call-time target won't fit the queue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I expect vacancies to close even if nobody announces a layoff. Three months saved gives us time, but I don't want to use it while a promised new role stays on paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'll ask for the figures on transferred calls and try the proven reply-checking tool on my own shift. In the first year, if a paid quality-check vacancy is posted at this centre or the one across town, I'll apply; otherwise I'll stay put.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, because I can picture fewer desks. I don't think my own wages disappear overnight, but the path gets narrower.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you take to the team meeting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd compare the count of complex calls with the old target and bring both to our team meeting. I need a number the manager can answer, not a speech about change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for training yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't spend our savings on a speculative course. If the employer offers paid hours to learn quality checking, I'll take them; otherwise I'll practise with the tools already on my shift.

say: I'd ask for **new call targets** if easy chats disappear.
I'd want **queue figures** before seats are cut.
think: I expect **unfilled vacancies** more than sudden layoffs as the centre moves easy chats onto software.
I won't spend our **savings** on an unposted role.
do: Compare **complex-call counts** with the old target this month.
Try the **reply-checking tool** on my own shift.
Apply for a **posted paid quality job** if one opens.
feel: **Uneasy** about fewer desks, while expecting my wage to continue for now.
S1.quote: I need a number the manager can answer, not a speech about change.
fieldNote: He wants **measured evidence** before accepting a staffing change.
His **training limit** protects shared savings from an uncertain payoff.
He sees a **local alternative** but will move only for a posted paid job.

steps.text: Try the proven reply-checking tool on his shift
Apply for a posted paid quality-check vacancy if available

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say the centre needs a schedule for what happens to agents when general AI handles calls by 2028. Robots around 2031 don't matter much to a headset and a chat screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my own role could go quickly, lead title or not. Our three months saved buys a short search, and my partner's bakery wage won't cover both our shares of the rent alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'll write down the complicated calls I resolve and ask the centre what paid audit vacancies might actually open. If I'm laid off in the first year after 2028, I'll apply for posted paid dispute jobs at the nearby service centres and use savings only for the gap after my partner's wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm alarmed. I can make a list of moves, but two years is not long for a whole field to shrink.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which household expense changes first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd cancel the weekend trips first, then review our rent before the savings ran out. I would not ask my partner to carry every bill without talking through a limit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the manager?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My shift colleagues and I would ask the manager to put notice terms in writing for everyone. A two-year date is close enough that each agent deserves the same answer.

say: I'd demand a **staffing schedule** before call work changes.
I'd say **2031 robots** do not protect our 2028 screen work.
think: I could lose my **lead role** quickly after general AI arrives.
Our **three-month reserve** and bakery wage cannot carry a long search.
do: Ask with **shift colleagues** for written notice terms this year.
Apply for **posted paid dispute jobs** after a real layoff.
Cancel **weekend trips** if my wages stop.
feel: **Alarmed** because local options may shrink at the same time.
S2.quote: Our three months saved buys a short search, and my partner's bakery wage won't cover both our shares of the rent alone.
fieldNote: He knows the **cushion has limits** if the whole occupation contracts.
He ties job applications to an **actual layoff** and posted pay.
He wants **common written notice** for every agent on the shift.

steps.text: Apply for posted paid dispute jobs if laid off
Cancel weekend trips if his wages stop
Ask with shift colleagues for common written notice terms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell colleagues five years lets us test a route into reviewing disputed accounts. We still face thinking AI in 2031; waiting for robots in 2034 would miss the point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could qualify for another desk role by then if the training has paid time and a real destination. I don't want to leave a decent wage for a certificate nobody is hiring for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll ask the two local service centres what their paid audit posts require. If my employer gives paid study hours, I'll complete the account-review module before 2031; in the first year after general AI, I'll apply for posted vacancies with wages at least close to mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious, but the calendar helps. Five years lets me test a route without draining our rent reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you judge whether the new role exists?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the other centres about actual job titles and starting pay, not just training brochures. Some of my colleagues may want different work, so I wouldn't prescribe one route for everyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if paid study hours never come?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the training is unpaid, I'll keep my shift and compare vacancy notices instead. My partner's bakery wage isn't a spare training fund.

say: I'd explore **account review** before 2031, but I want to know its wage and actual vacancies first.
I'd tell agents **2034 robots** arrive after our screen work changes.
think: I could gain a **new skill** with paid time and a real job destination.
I won't trade a **decent wage** for an unused certificate.
do: Check **local audit wages** and requirements this year.
Complete the **account-review module** only with paid study hours.
Apply for **posted wage-matched jobs** after 2031 if they exist.
feel: **Anxious**, yet helped by time to test the path.
S3.quote: My partner's bakery wage isn't a spare training fund.
fieldNote: He distinguishes a **paid job** from a training brochure.
His **module plan** depends on employer-paid time.
He values the **five-year runway** for checking options without using rent money.

steps.text: Complete account-review module if employer provides paid study hours
Apply for posted audit jobs with comparable pay after 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade gives the centre time to tell us what jobs will change and to fund transitions. Robots around 2039 are later than the thinking systems that would answer our calls in 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 27, I can build a second route by 2036 without giving up a job I like today. I still need the wages to be real. A long warning doesn't make rent optional.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Over the coming year I'll learn to check AI replies during one quality-review task on my shift if my manager approves the paid time and put part of regular pay into savings whenever the reserve dips below three months. If a posted paid role comes up before or during the first year after 2036, I'd compare its wage and only move if it covers our share of rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm. Ten years is enough for small, checked steps rather than a sudden leap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you check the market over ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would set a reminder every six months to compare paid vacancies and their requirements. If the same roles stay open, that would be better evidence than a prediction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would this change your plans with your partner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner and I wouldn't delay our ordinary plans on a headline from ten years away. We'd revisit the budget if my hours actually fell.

say: I'd ask the centre to **fund transitions** during the decade.
I'd separate **2036 call work** from robots expected around 2039.
think: I have **time** to build another route while still earning.
I need a **real wage** before moving jobs.
do: Learn to check **AI replies** during paid quality-review work if my manager approves it.
Rebuild our **three-month reserve** from regular pay if it dips.
Compare **posted paid jobs** twice yearly and move only if wages cover our share of rent.
feel: **Calm** with a decade for measured changes.
S4.quote: A long warning doesn't make rent optional.
fieldNote: His **long runway** allows experiments inside the current paid job.
He will judge **outside roles** by posted wages and rent coverage.
He treats the **reserve** as a household safeguard, not a training budget.

steps.text: Learn to check AI replies during approved paid quality-review work
Rebuild three-month reserve from pay if its balance dips
Compare posted paid jobs and move only if wages cover shared rent

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. Call work is thinking work, and three months of savings is short if local centres cut at the same time. Written notice for the whole shift and posted paid routes into dispute review would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what happens to the callers who cannot explain a charge in the neat words a bot expects. Callers who struggle to explain a charge often need a person to slow down. I would want the centre to count that time as work.

headlineQuote: Callers who struggle to explain a charge often need a person to slow down.
portrait: Omar is a **27-year-old lead** at a contact centre, with a two-year college diploma and strong disputed-bill skills.
He earns **typical pay**, shares expenses with a bakery worker and has about three months saved; some similar jobs are nearby.
He uses **AI occasionally** once it proves useful, and asks for measured staffing evidence before making a move.
The **2028 deadline** alarms him; five or ten years permits paid study and a careful comparison of actual vacancies.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could erase his call work before the shared reserve carries a long search.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice** for the full shift would show when income may change.
**Posted paid roles** in dispute review would give him an accountable route to apply.
